source.text: Ἀπεκαλύφθη δέ μοι, ἀδελφοί, κοιμωμένῳ ὑπὸ νεανίσκου εὐειδεστάτου λέγοντός μοι· Τὴν πρεσβυτέραν, παρ' ἧς ἔλαβες τὸ βιβλίδιον, τίνα δοκεῖς εἶναι; ἐγὼ φημί· Τὴν Σίβυλλαν. Πλανᾶσαι, φησίν, οὐκ ἔστιν. Τίς οὖν ἐστίν; φημί. Ἡ Ἐκκλησία, φησίν. εἶπον αὐτῷ· Διατί οὖν πρεσβυτέρα; Ὅτι, φησίν, πάντων πρώτη ἐκτίσθη· διὰ τοῦτο πρεσβυτέρα, καὶ διὰ ταύτην ὁ κόσμος κατηρτίσθη. 2. μετέπειτα δὲ ὅρασιν εἶδον ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ μου. ἦλθεν ἡ πρεσβυτέρα καὶ ἠρώτησέν με εἰ ἤδη τὸ βιβλίον δέδωκα τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις. ἠρνησάμην δεδωκέναι. Καλῶς, φησίν, πεποίηκας· ἔχω γὰρ ῥήματα προσθεῖναι. ὅταν οὖν ἀποτελέσω τὰ ῥήματα πάντα, διὰ σοῦ γνωρισθήσεται τοῖς ἐκλεκτοῖς πᾶσιν. 3. γράψεις οὖν δύο βιβλαρίδια, καὶ πέμψεις ἓν Κλήμεντι καὶ ἓν Γραπτῇ. πέμψει οὖν Κλήμης εἰς τὰς ἔξω πόλεις, ἐκείνῳ γὰρ ἐπιτέτραπται· Γραπτὴ δὲ νουθετήσει τὰς χήρας καὶ τοὺς ὀρφανούς. σὺ δὲ ἀναγνωσῇ εἰς ταύτην τὴν πόλιν μετὰ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων τῶν προϊσταμένων τῆς ἐκκλησίας.
source.label: Vision 2, section iv

translation.text:
And it was revealed to me, brothers[a], while I was asleep, by a very handsome young man who said to me: “The old woman[c], from whom you received the little book—who do you suppose she is?” I said, “The Sibyl[b].” “You are mistaken,” he says; “she is not.” “Then who is she?” I say. “The Church,” he says. I said to him, “Why then an old woman?” “Because,” he says, “she was created first of all; for this reason she is old, and for her sake the world was set in order[d][g].”

2. Afterward I saw a vision in my house. The old woman came and asked me whether I had already given the book to the elders[j]. I denied having given it. “You have done well,” she says; “for I have words to add. When, therefore, I complete all the words, through you they will be made known to all the elect.

3. “So you will write two little booklets, and you will send one to Clement[h] and one to Grapte[i]. Then Clement will send it to the cities outside[e], for this has been entrusted to him; but Grapte will admonish the widows and the orphans. But you will read it aloud[f] in this city together with the elders[j] who preside over the church.”

translation.text:
And it was revealed to me[k], brothers[a], while I was asleep, by a very handsome young man who said to me: “The old woman[c], from whom you received the little book—who do you think she is?” I said, “The Sibyl[b].” “You are mistaken,” he says; “she is not.” “Then who is she?” I say. “The Church,” he says. I said to him, “Why then is she old?” “Because,” he says, “she was created first of all; for this reason she is old, and for her sake the world was formed[d][g].”

2. Afterward I saw a vision in my house. The old woman came and asked me whether I had already given the book to the elders[j]. I denied having given it. “You have done well,” she says; “for I have words to add. When, therefore, I complete all the words, through you they will be made known to all the elect.

3. “So you will write two little booklets, and you will send one to Clement[h] and one to Grapte[i]. Then Clement will send it to the cities outside[e], for this has been entrusted to him; but Grapte will admonish the widows and the orphans. But you will read it aloud[f] in this city with the elders[j] who preside over the church.”

footnotes.text: “Brothers” (ἀδελφοί) is a standard communal address in early Christian texts and is inclusive of the whole assembly, men and women.
The Sibyl was a well-known figure of pagan prophetic oracles in the Greco-Roman world; Hermas’s first guess situates his vision in that cultural landscape.
Greek πρεσβυτέρα can mean “elder/older woman.” Rendered here as “old woman” to distinguish from the office term πρεσβύτεροι (“elders”) appearing later.
“Was set in order” translates κατηρτίσθη; alternatives include “was prepared,” “was fashioned,” “was established.”
“Cities outside” likely means cities outside Rome, suggesting a distribution network beyond the local church.
The verb ἀναγινώσκω ordinarily refers to public reading; hence “read it aloud.”
Hermas depicts the Church as primordial and creation as ordered for her sake; compare Jewish Wisdom traditions (e.g., Proverbs 8:22–31), while noting Hermas explicitly names the Church.
Clement may refer to a leading figure in the Roman church tasked with external correspondence; the text does not specify further identity.
Grapte is a woman charged with instructing widows and orphans—an early witness to structured care and teaching for vulnerable members.
“Elders” (πρεσβύτεροι) are recognized local leaders; “who preside” (προΐσταμαι) indicates formal oversight of the church.
Or 'through you they will be made known to all the elect.”'.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Standard passive of apokalyptō in visionary contexts emphasizes divine revelation rather than mere showing.
Vocative address to the community; retained as “brothers” to preserve second-century idiom, with a note indicating inclusive reference.
Temporal participle; “asleep” concise and natural in English narrative.
Superlative εὐειδεστάτου rendered as “very handsome” to keep intensity while maintaining idiomatic English.
Descriptive of age; “old woman” avoids confusion with the office term πρεσβύτεροι (elders) later in the passage.
Diminutive; “little book” keeps concreteness without committing to scroll vs. codex form.
Proper name for a famed pagan prophetess; transliterated.
Idiomatic rebuke; maintains force without archaism.
Second-century Christian usage denotes the Church; capitalized due to personification as a woman.
Creation term; preserves theological weight of first-created claim.
Captures arranging/ordering nuance rather than mere making; suits the cosmic-order sense.
Technical term for a visionary experience.
Technical term for church office; “elders” is standard and compact.
Plural rhema; concrete “words” keeps the serial, additive sense.
Teleological nuance preserved succinctly with “complete.”
Passive of gnōrizō; distinct from “reveal,” maintaining verbal variety.
Preserves technical theological term; concise and traditional without importing later doctrinal specificity.
Diminutive plural; “booklets” naturally conveys small size.
Literal spatial sense relative to the sender’s city; footnote clarifies likely referent (outside Rome).
Connotes responsibility given to Clement; “entrusted” fits ecclesial delegation.
Paraenetic term with moral edge; stronger than mere instruction, fitting Hermas’s tone.
Anaginoskō typically denotes public reading; explicit “aloud” preserves communal practice.
Presiding leadership nuance; maintains early church order language without modernization.

theological_decisions.issue: Identity of the woman in the vision
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: She is the Church (personified), not the Sibyl.
alternative_readings: A symbolic wise woman (e.g., Wisdom personified)
theological_decisions.rationale: The text explicitly identifies her as ἡ Ἐκκλησία; preserving the identification anchors the ecclesial allegory central to Hermas.

theological_decisions.issue: Reason the Church appears as an old woman
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: She appears old because she was created first of all, and for her sake the world was set in order.
alternative_readings: Purely metaphorical for the Church’s antiquity/pre-eminence without ontological claim
Allusion to Wisdom traditions rather than a doctrinal assertion
theological_decisions.rationale: We render the claim as stated, preserving Hermas’s tension-laden pre-existence imagery without harmonizing or softening it.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate as “the Church,” capitalized in context.
theological_decisions.rationale: Second-century Roman Christian context and personification support the ecclesial sense; capitalization signals the personified figure.

theological_decisions.issue: Public reading practice implied by ἀναγινώσκω
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render “you will read it aloud,” reflecting communal liturgical reading.
theological_decisions.rationale: Early Christian texts were read publicly; making this explicit preserves the ecclesial setting and practice.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: “the elect” to preserve the theological term.
theological_decisions.rationale: Maintains traditional theological vocabulary without specifying a particular doctrinal system; alternatives are noted in lexical options.

theological_decisions.issue: Church order in “elders who preside over the church”
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Maintain presiding/leadership language rather than generic ‘leaders.’
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas reflects emerging church order; “preside” preserves the technical flavor of προΐσταμαι.

review_passes.summary: The draft is generally excellent and captures the register well. However, there are a few minor issues: a grammatical hypercorrection ('whom' instead of 'who'), a missed neuter-plural agreement ('it' instead of 'they' for 'the words'), a slightly flattened verb ('said I had not' instead of 'denied'), and a couple of missed or under-translated conjunctions (οὖν, δὲ) that help structure the final instructions.
issues_found: Grammar: 'whom do you suppose she is?' uses 'whom' incorrectly for the predicate nominative; it should be 'who'.
Lexical: 'I said I had not given it' slightly flattens 'ἠρνησάμην' (I denied). 'I denied having given it' is more direct and accurate to the Greek.

Grammar: 'it will be made known' fails to recognize that the singular Greek verb 'γνωρισθήσεται' is agreeing with the neuter plural subject 'τὰ ῥήματα πάντα' (all the words). In English, this must be plural: 'they will be made known'.
Missing nuance: 'You will write' misses the inferential conjunction 'οὖν' (so/therefore) in 'γράψεις οὖν'.
Missing nuance: 'And you will read it aloud' translates 'σὺ δὲ' as 'And', but 'But' better captures the contrast with the distinct tasks assigned to Clement and Grapte.

Πλανᾶσαι, φησίν, οὐκ ἔστιν. Τίς οὖν ἐστίν; φημί. Ἡ Ἐκκλησία, φησίν. εἶπον αὐτῷ· Διατί οὖν πρεσβυτέρα; Ὅτι, φησίν, πάντων πρώτη ἐκτίσθη· διὰ τοῦτο πρεσβυτέρα, καὶ διὰ ταύτην ὁ κόσμος κατηρτίσθη. 2. μετέπειτα δὲ ὅρασιν εἶδον ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ μου. ἦλθεν ἡ πρεσβυτέρα καὶ ἠρώτησέν με εἰ ἤδη τὸ βιβλίον δέδωκα τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις. ἠρνησάμην δεδωκέναι. Καλῶς, φησίν, πεποίηκας· ἔχω γὰρ ῥήματα προσθεῖναι. ὅταν οὖν ἀποτελέσω τὰ ῥήματα πάντα, διὰ σοῦ γνωρισθήσεται τοῖς ἐκλεκτοῖς πᾶσιν. 3. γράψεις οὖν δύο βιβλαρίδια, καὶ πέμψεις ἓν Κλήμεντι καὶ ἓν Γραπτῇ. πέμψει οὖν Κλήμης εἰς τὰς ἔξω πόλεις, ἐκείνῳ γὰρ ἐπιτέτραπται· Γραπτὴ δὲ νουθετήσει τὰς χήρας καὶ τοὺς ὀρφανούς. σὺ δὲ ἀναγνωσῇ εἰς ταύτην τὴν πόλιν μετὰ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων τῶν προϊσταμένων τῆς ἐκκλησίας.

base_translation.text: And it was revealed to me, brothers, while I was asleep, by a very handsome young man who said to me: “The old woman, from whom you received the little book—who do you think she is?” I said, “The Sibyl.” “You are mistaken,” he says; “she is not.” “Then who is she?” I say. “The Church,” he says. I said to him, “Why then is she old?” “Because,” he says, “she was created first of all; for this reason she is old, and for her sake the world was formed.”

translation.text:
Brothers, while I was asleep, I received a revelation. A very handsome young man asked me, “Who do you think the old woman is—the one who gave you the little book?”

“The Sibyl,” I answered.

“You are mistaken,” he said. “She is not the Sibyl.”

“Then who is she?” I asked.

“The Church,” he replied.

“Why, then, is she old?” I asked.

“Because she was created before everything else,” he said. “That is why she is old, and the world was formed for her sake.”

translation.text: 2. Later, while I was at home, I saw another vision. The old woman came and asked whether I had given the book to the elders yet. I told her I had not. She said, “You did well, because I still have words to add. When I have finished giving you all the words, you will make them known to all God’s chosen people.”

simplification_decisions.reasoning_layer_used: POB text and immediate narrative context

spob_revision_history.previous_text: 3. “Write two small books. Send one to Clement and the other to Grapte. Clement will send his copy to the other cities, since he has been given this responsibility. Grapte will instruct the widows and orphans. You must read your copy aloud here in the city, together with the elders who lead the church.”
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The draft is generally clearer and its direct commands, plain explanation of Clement’s entrusted task, and “elders who lead the church” are warranted simplifications. However, “your copy” resolves an acknowledged ambiguity by asserting a third local manuscript, and “instruct” weakens the admonitory function assigned to Grapte. The replacement retains accessible wording without adding the disputed physical-copy detail or reducing admonition to generic instruction.
